analysis.investment_thesis: JSW Dulux is a genuinely high-quality paints business carrying the Dulux brand (AkzoNobel's global crown jewel) with extraordinary capital returns — ROE of 32.3% and ROCE of 41.6% — and a near-debt-free balance sheet, characteristics I associate with businesses that have true pricing power and customer loyalty. However, revenue has compounded at only 5% over nine years and the current 35x P/E is a price I find difficult to justify for that pace of growth, making this a business I admire but would want cheaper before buying aggressively.
key_strengths: ROE of 32.3% and ROCE of 41.6% are exceptional — few businesses on any exchange in the world deploy capital this efficiently, signaling genuine brand-driven pricing power
Essentially debt-free (INR 71 Cr borrowings against INR 2,256 Cr equity), meaning every rupee of profit belongs to shareholders without a finance cost claim — this is a balance sheet I love
Operating income growing at 10.6% CAGR with consistent margin expansion — the business is becoming more profitable per rupee of revenue, not less
key_risks: Revenue CAGR of just 5% over nine years is underwhelming for a branded consumer business — Asian Paints and Berger have outpaced this significantly, suggesting Dulux has not won sufficient market share

At 35.2x P/E with only 8.1% net profit CAGR, investors are paying a substantial premium that requires accelerated growth to justify — any disappointment in volumes will compress the multiple painfully

JSW Group's acquisition of AkzoNobel India introduces integration risk and potential for strategic misalignment between a global chemical giant's brand and an Indian industrial conglomerate's priorities
red_flags: FCF declined to INR 204 Cr in FY2025 from INR 367-382 Cr range in prior years — capital expenditure is accelerating (CWIP rising from INR 16 Cr to INR 74 Cr) and consuming free cash generation

The Dulux brand competes directly against Asian Paints — one of India's finest businesses — in a market where the incumbent's distribution network and brand loyalty create a very high bar for challengers
P/B of 10x offers no margin of safety if growth disappoints; the stock price embeds near-perfection in execution
analysis.detailed_analysis:
If I could own this business at 20x earnings, I would be very interested. The hallmarks are all present: a recognizable global brand (Dulux), capital-light manufacturing with FMCG-like return ratios, zero dependence on debt financing, and a management team that is expanding operating margins steadily. The gross margin of 89.6% is extraordinary — this is not a business that competes on price, it competes on the confidence a homeowner feels pointing to a Dulux-painted wall.

The hesitation is entirely about price. At 35.2x P/E for a business growing earnings at 8%, I am paying 4.4x the growth rate — a premium that requires either an acceleration in revenue growth (which nine years of 5% CAGR does not promise) or a permanent re-rating of the multiple. I have been taught that time is the friend of a wonderful business and the enemy of a mediocre one; JSW Dulux is clearly wonderful, but I would rather wait for Mr. Market to offer me this business at a fairer price. It belongs on my watchlist, not yet in my portfolio.
